title: Loop back: edge cases and guards
idea: LOOP. No new concept. Review the edge-case habit: zero, empty, and boundary values handled with a guard before the main logic.

exercises.explanation: count is 0, so the guard runs first and prints the special message. (Review of zero guards.)

exercises.prompt: Handling the zero or empty case first is a good habit before the main calculation.
exercises.explanation: A guard catches the tricky edge up front so the main logic stays simple. (Review of edge-case habit.)

exercises.prompt: Why guard against dividing when a count is 0?
options: Dividing by zero is an error, so you handle 0 separately
exercises.explanation: You cannot divide by zero, so the 0 case needs its own branch. (Review of guards.)

exercises.prompt: A shop gives free shipping for 'spend 50 or more'. For exactly 50, which test is correct?
exercises.explanation: '50 or more' includes 50, so >=. Using > would wrongly charge the exact-50 cart. (Review of boundaries.)
== 0 catches the empty order before the main case. (Review of == and guards.)

exercises.prompt: Which value is the trickiest to test for a '% 2 == 0' even check?
options: 0 - make sure 0 is treated as even
exercises.explanation: 0 % 2 is 0, so 0 is even - an easy edge to overlook. Test it on purpose. (Review of edge testing.)

exercises.prompt: A program that works for typical inputs is guaranteed to work for edge values like 0 or the exact boundary.
exercises.explanation: Edges often behave differently. Always test 0, empty, and boundary values. (Review of edge-case habit.)
3 is not <= 0, so the else uses an f-string: '3 left'. The guard protects the empty case. (Review of guards + f-strings.)

exercises.prompt: For the stock code above, what prints when stock = 0?
exercises.explanation: 0 <= 0 is true, so the guard runs: 'Out of stock'. The edge is handled correctly. (Review of boundary guards.)
